title: Monitor budgets related to community projects

lessons.title: Understanding the project budget
lessons.html:
Why budgets matter in community projects

Community projects such as a communal vegetable garden, a LandCare erosion project, a poultry co-operative or a borehole and irrigation scheme are often funded by government grants, donors or corporate social investment. Funders expect money to be spent on what was agreed, and members expect fairness and transparency. Poor budget control is one of the most common reasons community projects fail or lose funding.

Parts of a budget

  • Income – grants, member contributions, loans, sales of produce, in-kind contributions (donated labour, land, equipment).
  • Capital expenditure – once-off assets: fencing, tanks, pumps, tunnels, tools.
  • Operating expenditure – recurring costs: seed, fertiliser, feed, fuel, electricity, transport, stipends, repairs.
  • Contingency – a reserve for unexpected costs (often a small percentage, if the funder allows).

Budget line items and periods

Each budget line has a code, a description, the approved amount and the period. Break the annual budget into a monthly or quarterly cash flow forecast, because agricultural spending is seasonal: inputs are bought before planting, income comes after harvest.

LineApproved (R)Q1Q2Q3Q4
Seed and seedlings18 0009 00009 0000
Fertiliser and compost12 0006 00006 0000
Drip irrigation repairs8 0002 0002 0002 0002 000

Roles

Clarify who may approve spending (usually two signatories), who keeps records (treasurer or bookkeeper), who checks (the committee and, for larger projects, an auditor), and what the funder's reporting requirements are. Make sure everyone has a copy of the approved budget in plain language.

lessons.title: Tracking spending and variances
lessons.html:
Record every transaction

  • Keep a cash book or simple spreadsheet: date, description, budget line, amount, supplier, and document reference.
  • Get quotations (often three for larger purchases) and keep them with the order.
  • Keep invoices, receipts and proof of payment for every rand spent. No receipt, no reimbursement.
  • Use a dedicated project bank account. Avoid cash where possible; if petty cash is needed, keep a petty cash book with a float and slips.
  • Reconcile the cash book with the bank statement every month.

Comparing budget to actual

Each month or quarter, compare actual spending with the budget for each line. The difference is the variance.

LineBudget to date (R)Actual to date (R)Variance (R)%
Seed and seedlings9 00010 800-1 800 (over)20% over
Fertiliser6 0004 500+1 500 (under)25% under

Variance % = variance ÷ budget × 100. Agree a threshold (for example 10%) above which the committee must discuss the cause.

Investigating variances

  • Price change? (Seed prices rose.)
  • Timing? (Fertiliser not yet bought, so it is not a real saving.)
  • Scope change? (Extra beds planted.)
  • Error or misuse? (Wrong line coded, or unauthorised spending.)

Over-spending on one line may be covered by moving funds from another (a virement), but only if the funder's rules allow and with written approval.

lessons.title: Reporting and accountability
lessons.html:
Financial reports

A good monthly or quarterly report to the committee and funder includes:

  1. Budget versus actual per line, with variances.
  2. Explanations for significant variances and actions taken.
  3. Bank balance and reconciliation.
  4. Cash flow forecast for the next period.
  5. Progress on outputs (e.g. hectares planted, metres of fence built), so spending is linked to results.

Transparency with members

Present a simple summary at general meetings, using charts or a poster if literacy levels vary. Allow members to ask questions. Transparency builds trust and reduces conflict.

Warning signs of fraud or mismanagement

  • Missing receipts or altered documents
  • One person controlling ordering, paying and recording
  • Payments to suppliers linked to committee members (conflict of interest)
  • Bank reconciliations not done

Controls such as segregation of duties, two signatories, and regular independent checks protect both the project and honest office-bearers. Report suspected fraud to the funder and, where necessary, the police.

Key points

  • A budget has income, capital, operating and contingency lines, broken into a seasonal cash flow.
  • Keep source documents for every transaction and reconcile monthly.
  • Variance = budget minus actual; investigate variances above an agreed threshold.
  • Move funds between lines only with funder approval.
  • Report regularly and transparently, and use controls to prevent fraud.
